posts.title: A finance chief for a family-owned logistics group
posts.excerpt: How Senbatsu Partners placed an unadvertised chief financial officer for a multi-generational European logistics group in thirteen weeks.
posts.content:
When the supervisory board of a multi-generational logistics group with operations spanning the Benelux and Germany faced the planned retirement of their chief financial officer, they recognized that the appointment carried profound structural implications. The business had grown steadily over four decades, maintaining conservative debt levels and close relationships with European banking syndicates. However, modernizing warehouse automation, navigating fleet decarbonization, and preparing reporting systems for new corporate sustainability standards required a financial executive with sophisticated institutional experience. The family owners were adamant about one thing: the new chief financial officer had to respect the company's patient, generational perspective while executing rigorous modernization.

Senbatsu Partners was retained to lead the search. In week 0, founding partner Helena Marsh and a second partner spent a half day at the client's regional headquarters conducting our mandatory brief session. Together with the family board and the chief executive, we defined the leadership mandate and articulated the clear line we would not cross. In this search, the boundary was twofold: we would not approach financial leaders from the client's primary transport customers, nor would we accept candidates accustomed only to short-term private equity cycles where debt engineering takes precedence over operational continuity. The resulting one-page role brief gave our team an unambiguous foundation.

During weeks 1 to 4, Jonas Weber led research to map the European freight, supply chain, and contract logistics sectors, constructing a market map of about 60 qualified financial leaders. The search deliberately avoided public postings and focused on high-performing finance chiefs and regional corporate controllers who were not actively seeking new employment. Through quiet, discrete direct inquiries, Helena Marsh evaluated candidate track records in treasury management, complex ERP transitions, and capital expenditure oversight. Candidate suitability was measured against the specific governance criteria established in the signed brief.

By week 6, Helena presented a shortlist of 3 candidates to the supervisory board. Each of the three finalists had been interviewed in person, evaluated against the brief criteria, and referenced twice through discreet professional backchannels by our associate Priya Raman. Crucially, all three confirmed their active interest in the family group's long-term mandate and compensation structure. None of them had been on the open job market. The eventual preferred candidate was serving as group controller of an international industrial group, leading a multinational finance division while successfully preserving family shareholder trust.

Interviews and confidential stakeholder meetings proceeded smoothly through weeks 7 to 11. Associate Priya Raman completed extensive referencing calls to examine leadership temperament, banking relationships, and decision-making during past downturns. When formal offer terms were finalized in week 13, Helena Marsh attended the negotiation in person to ensure complete clarity regarding base salary, performance targets, and relocation arrangements. From the initial brief session to a signed employment agreement, the mandate concluded in 13 weeks. As with all our retained searches, structured follow-up reviews were conducted at 3, 6, and 12 months, confirming that the new finance chief had successfully integrated into the executive committee while maintaining strong trust with the family board.

posts.title: General counsel for a listed medical-device maker
posts.excerpt: Appointing a General Counsel in 11 weeks while strictly holding our line of making no approaches to current clients.
posts.content:
A listed maker of medical devices needed a general counsel who had run compliance through an inspection cycle. In the brief session the board set one condition: no candidates from companies that were already our clients. We wrote it into the brief and held it for the whole search, which narrowed the market map but not the quality of the shortlist.

Three people were presented in week 6, each met in person and referenced twice. The interviews and references ran from week 7 to week 10, and the signed offer arrived in week 11. The partner who led the search was present at the offer conversation, as in every search we run.

posts.title: A plant director who was not looking
posts.excerpt: Securing a head of plant operations in 16 weeks and resolving regional relocation within the region.
posts.content:
An industrial group needed a head of plant operations for a site in the south of the region. The brief was clear on skills and unusually honest about the location: the person would have to move within the region. That made the search slower than most, and we said so at the brief session.

The shortlist of 3 was presented in week 6. The person who accepted had not applied anywhere in years. We met her twice, referenced her twice, and spent most of weeks 7 to 11 on the practical questions of moving a family. The offer was signed in week 16, with a partner at the table.

posts.title: How we write a role brief
posts.excerpt: The half-day session and the one-page brief that every search starts from.
posts.content:
Every search starts with a half-day session at the client, led by two partners. We ask what the seat is for, who it reports to, what it must change in the first year and who will be in the room when the offer is made. We also ask for the line you will not cross: the names, companies or kinds of approach that are off limits.

The result is a one-page brief that the client signs off before anyone is approached. It is the document we measure the shortlist against, and the reason a shortlist of 3 is usually enough.
